question: What is the theoretical maximum ethanol yield on glucose according to the Yeast9 and iMM904 genome-scale models, and how close do measured ethanol yields come to it?

claims.text: Flux balance analysis of the Yeast9 genome-scale model gives a theoretical maximum ethanol yield on glucose, computed as the most product the network can make from that sugar, with no time axis or vessel.

Flux balance analysis of the iMM904 genome-scale model gives a theoretical maximum ethanol yield on glucose, computed as the most product the network can make from that sugar, with no time axis or vessel.
The Yeast9 and iMM904 glucose-to-ethanol ceilings agree with each other in both mass and molar units, since both models route ethanol through pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase.

gaps: Every measured record returned is an unverified extractor candidate with no provenance-checked strain, oxygen regime, or sugar concentration in most rows, so the comparison to the ceiling is indicative only.

Closeness to the ceiling is not stated as a fraction in any record; a reader would need the measured yields reported on the same basis (g per g glucose, anaerobic batch, unit-consumption basis) side by side with the ceiling, ideally from verified records with conditions.

No verified record gives an anaerobic, glucose-limited, batch ethanol yield with its strain and temperature, so the best-performing measured yield in the strain-engineering literature cannot be placed reliably relative to the ceiling.

The ceiling is a flux balance result, not a fermentation measurement; it assumes no biomass formation and no glycerol or other by-product drain, so measured yields below it are expected and their gap reflects growth and by-product costs that the record set does not quantify.
